title: The Price of Work and the Worth of Work
text:
Imagine a home health aide we will never meet. She spends her mornings helping a man who has had a stroke get dressed, take his medications, and stay out of a nursing home for one more month. Somewhere across town, a junior analyst at an investment bank will earn more in his year-end bonus than she earns in a year. If I imagine a society that cared about broadly shared income and wealth, and about equal pay and outcomes across race and gender, I can’t make that ordering come out right. It looks upside down. And yet it is no accident, and I’m not even sure it is a malfunction. So the question I want to sit with is how a pay structure this far out of step with what people contribute comes to exist, and why it stays put.
The answer most of us learned in an introductory economics class is scarcity. Wages, we were told, reflect how rare a skill is relative to how much people want it. Surgeons are rare; cashiers are not. I find this argument genuinely interesting, and I think it is partly true. My suspicion is that it explains less than it seems to. It describes how prices move once a field of conditions is already in place, and it says very little about who arranged the field.
The careful version of the scarcity argument deserves its due, because it is better than the slogan. It doesn’t claim that rare things are simply expensive. It claims that a wage reflects what one more hour of a worker’s labor is worth to whoever is buying it, compared with how many other people could supply that hour. Economists call this the marginal revenue product of labor, a phrase only an economist could love. On this account, a nurse’s pay is held down by the reimbursement caps hospitals face from insurers and public programs, however scarce nurses happen to be. The hedge fund analyst, meanwhile, needn’t be a rare genius. She simply sits beside an enormous pile of capital, so a small improvement in her judgment is worth millions to someone.
Notice what has happened, though. Once we admit that wages track the value of labor to a buyer, we have already conceded that wages measure something other than contribution to the common good. A buyer’s valuation depends on what the buyer wants and on how much money the buyer has. Scarcity is never scarcity in the abstract. It is always scarcity relative to a particular arrangement of demand, and that arrangement was built out of earlier distributions of wealth, power, and esteem. If I want to understand pay, it seems I have to understand those.
Start with demand. Markets register what economists call effective demand, which is a polite way of saying wants backed by money. A need that nobody can pay for doesn’t show up as demand at all. As far as the market can see, it simply isn’t there. A wealthy household’s desire for a kitchen renovation or a private tutor counts in full, dollar for dollar. A poor neighborhood’s need for childcare, mental health services, or a bus that comes on time counts only as far as its residents, or a government acting for them, can pay. I suspect this is the deepest reason pay drifts away from contribution. The wage structure is, in part, a mirror held up to the existing distribution of wealth. Where money gathers, the work that serves money is well paid. Where need gathers without money, the work that meets that need is underpaid, underfunded, or left undone.
What unsettles me is that this is the market doing exactly what it was designed to do. It aggregates preferences weighted by purchasing power, and it does so very efficiently. That design reflects a choice about what an economy is for. Over the last several decades, the United States has increasingly treated financial return as the measure of value. Tax law has favored capital gains over wages, corporate governance has prized shareholder return, and public goods like a sturdy safety net, universal childcare, or well-funded schools have been treated as costs to trim. Under those priorities, work that produces social goods without producing a revenue stream will be paid less. Teachers, social workers, public defenders, and Medicaid-funded care workers are paid out of budgets, which means their wages are policy decisions. Somebody, somewhere, decided this is what their work is worth to us.
A related pattern has to do with where a job sits. Some jobs sit beside great rivers of money, and it turns out that dipping a small cup into a very large river still fills a very large bucket. Corporate lawyers, investment bankers, private equity partners, and senior executives stand where enormous sums flow past. Their pay seems to reflect the size of what they touch more than the size of what they make.
Compare a teacher. Over a lifetime, a good teacher’s contribution may be immense: higher earnings for her students, better health, more participation in civic life. For all that, her contribution is diffuse. It is spread across decades and thousands of people, it is hard to attribute to her, and it never arrives as a revenue stream an employer can capture and share. The teacher creates value that society absorbs. The banker handles value that can be skimmed. The market, being a market, rewards the banker.
The supply side of the story turns out to be less natural than it looks, too. Many high-paying professions are scarce partly because entry is deliberately restricted. Licensing, credential requirements, limited training slots, and immigration rules all shape how many people may do a given job. The number of medical residency positions in the United States has long been held down by federal funding rules, which in turn limits how many physicians the country produces. Bar exams and professional accreditation do similar work in other fields. Some of this guards real goods like public safety. Some of it mostly guards incomes. I don’t know where the line falls in every case, and I doubt anyone does. Either way, scarcity here is at least partly made by institutions. It is worth noticing, too, that the jobs with the fewest such protections, home care and food service and farm labor among them, are disproportionately done by women, immigrants, and workers of color. The power to manufacture scarcity is itself unevenly shared.
Of everything here, the evidence that most convinces me that pay carries cultural judgment comes from the sociologist Paula England and her work on the devaluation of women’s work. The basic pattern is well established. Occupations with a higher share of women pay less than those with fewer women, even after accounting for the education and skill the jobs require. The question is why.
Two stories compete. The queuing story says pay drives gender composition: when a job’s pay or conditions decline, men leave, and women, who often face narrower options, fill the gap. The devaluation story runs the other way. When a job fills with women, employers and the wider culture start to see the work as less skilled and less valuable, and pay follows that perception downward.
In 2009, Asaf Levanon, Paula England, and Paul Allison tested these stories in Social Forces using U.S. Census data from 1950 to 2000. Because they could follow the same occupations over time, they could watch what happened to pay as each occupation’s gender mix changed. They found substantial support for devaluation and very little for queuing. As women moved into an occupation, its pay tended to fall afterward. Coverage of the study pointed to recreation work and ticket agents, both of which shifted from mostly male to mostly female and saw their relative wages drop sharply. Computer programming tells the same story in reverse. It began as clerical work largely done by women, and as it became male-dominated and prestigious, the pay rose with it.
Observational data can never entirely rule out a hidden third factor, and I want to be careful here. A 2026 survey experiment by England, Levanon, and colleagues took that worry seriously. They described the same occupation to different respondents, changing only its gender composition. When people were told a job was mostly done by women, they recommended lower pay for it than when they were told it was mixed or mostly male. The work was identical. Only its association with women changed. I can’t think of a cleaner demonstration that wages carry cultural judgments.
The devaluation seems to reach beyond gender to the kind of work itself. England and others have documented a care penalty: jobs that involve caring for people pay less than their skill demands would predict, whether men or women do them. Care is coded as feminine, as something done out of love or nature, and so as something that shouldn’t need to be paid well. That coding carries a racial history as well. Domestic and agricultural labor, much of it done by Black women and immigrants, was deliberately left out of early New Deal labor protections, and the echo of that exclusion still sounds in how we pay for care.
Where does this leave the scarcity argument? Somewhere smaller, I think. Scarcity operates, but it operates inside a field already shaped by who holds wealth, whose needs count as demand, which jobs sit near the money, which professions can close their doors, and which kinds of work a culture has learned to discount. A defender of markets could reasonably answer that these are distortions to be corrected, and that markets still gather information better than any planner could. I take that answer seriously. It also seems to concede the point I care about. The wage structure looks much less like a neutral measurement of value and much more like a record of social choices about whose work matters. If that is right, it could be chosen differently. Whether we have the will to choose differently is a question I can’t answer here.

title: Eric Eliot Schnitger’s Portfolio
text:
I once gave a conference talk called “Why Isn’t Everyone Paid Enough?” I’m still working on the answer, now with Python.
I wrote a dissertation on complicity in capitalism, taught for a while, and attained the holy grail of American life, health insurance, by working retail. I’m a researcher and analyst interested in economic justice, climate, and what an economy looks like when it stops treating growth as the point. I trained as an ethicist, which taught me to ask better questions. I learned SQL, R, and Tableau so I could test the answers against data, which turned out to be its own rabbit hole.
This site is where the projects and writing end up. My resume lives on the About page. It’s a fun read.

Era-by-Era Breakdown

Pre-Abramovich (1992-2003): The Fergie Monopoly
The early Premier League was dominated by a single manager. Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United won 8 of 11 titles, but the points required to win were not exceptionally high (average: ~83 pts). The league was competitive enough that Blackburn (1995) and Arsenal (1998, 2002, 2004) could break through.
Relegation survival averaged ~39 points, notably higher than any subsequent era. The financial gap between top and bottom had not yet become a chasm.


The Oligarch Era (2003-2016): Money Changes Everything
Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea in 2003 marked a turning point. Then Manchester City’s 2008 takeover created a third “super-club.” Title-winning points climbed to an average of ~88 pts, while relegation survival drifted down to ~35 points.
The Leicester miracle (2015/16, 81 pts) was the exception that proved the rule.

Methodology & Technical Notes






NoteTechnical details (click to expand)





Data source: Scraped from Wikipedia’s individual season articles using requests and pandas.read_html(). Team names are cleaned of citation markers, qualification tags, and Unicode artifacts.
Caching: Results are cached to a local CSV (pl_data_cache.csv) with a 7-day expiry to avoid unnecessary requests to Wikipedia. The freeze: auto setting in Quarto further ensures the notebook only re-executes when source code changes.
Rate limiting: A 1.5-second delay between requests respects Wikipedia’s usage guidelines.
22-team seasons: The first three seasons (1992/93 through 1994/95) had 22 teams. Relegation positions are adjusted accordingly (19th survived, 20th-22nd relegated).
Champions League qualification: The number of CL spots changed over time (1 in the early 1990s, gradually expanding to 4 by 2001/02). This analysis consistently tracks the top 4 finishers regardless of how many actually qualified for the Champions League in that era.
Trend lines: Linear regression via numpy.polyfit(x, y, 1), calculated independently per era.









NoteWhat I’d Explore Next (click to expand)






Revenue correlation: Does the gap track with TV deal sizes? The 2016/17 season (start of the current mega-deal) aligns with the gap widening.
Wage bill ratio: How closely does the points gap mirror the spending gap?
Promotion bounce-back rate: Of the clubs relegated, how quickly (if ever) do they return?
European comparison: Do La Liga, Bundesliga, and Serie A show the same stratification, or is this a Premier League-specific phenomenon?

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Every year each state reports to the Federal Highway Administration what its highway agency spent on capital projects, and what kind of work the money paid for. This project pulls those reports for 2012 to 2024 and asks three questions. How much goes to repaving and repairing the roads that already exist? What is that money worth once rising construction prices are taken out? And how many miles of road does it cover?
The spending reports do not single out resurfacing. Most states fold it into a broader line, so the spending measure is FHWA’s “3R” group: resurfacing, restoration, rehabilitation, and minor widening.

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Every year each state reports to the Federal Highway Administration what its highway agency spent on capital projects, and what kind of work the money paid for. This project pulls those reports for 2012 to 2024 and asks three questions. How much goes to repaving and repairing the roads that already exist? What is that money worth once rising construction prices are taken out? And how many miles of road does it cover?
The spending reports do not single out resurfacing. Most states fold it into a broader line, so the spending measure is FHWA’s “3R” group: resurfacing, restoration, rehabilitation, and minor widening.

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Key Findings

Spending rose on paper. States spent $35.1 billion on 3R work in 2024, against $18.0 billion in 2012.
Prices rose faster. Highway construction prices rose 102% over the same years. In 2024 prices, 3R spending fell 3% between 2012 and 2024, and it peaked in 2020.
The share held steady. 3R work took 33% of state highway capital spending in 2024, against 27% in 2012. It is the largest single use of the money.
Fewer miles, and fewer miles per dollar. Federal-aid repaving projects covered 54,079 miles in 2012 and 31,308 in 2024. A million dollars, in 2024 prices, covered 2.6 miles in 2012 and 1.9 in 2024.

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Reading the Numbers

Inflation adjustment. Dollars are restated in 2024 prices using FHWA’s National Highway Construction Cost Index, averaged over each calendar year.
Two different sets of projects. Spending comes from what state highway agencies paid out. Miles come from projects with federal-aid funds authorized that fiscal year, and are divided only by those projects’ own costs. The two charts should not be combined.
Miles per dollar is not only about prices. Prices are already taken out, so a fall can also mean heavier work per mile, more urban and multi-lane roads, or more safety and drainage work inside the same project. The table counts centerline miles, not lane-miles.
State agencies only. What cities and counties spend on their own streets is not in these reports.
Local-class roads are left out of spending. They only appear in the table from 2015, so they are dropped to keep every year comparable.
Gaps and reused figures. FHWA published no miles table in its 2021 edition. When a state does not report, FHWA carries its previous year’s numbers forward.

title: How Much Do States Spend Repaving Roads?
text:
Data and Code
The sources are FHWA Highway Statistics Tables SF-12A and FA-10, one workbook per year, and FHWA’s National Highway Construction Cost Index. The data notebook downloads them, reads every sheet, and checks each column against the totals FHWA publishes before any figure is used.
The code is on GitHub.

title: Marriage, Religion, and Politics by County
text:
Overview
This is the first step in a larger project on how people form lasting relationships in the United States, and what the places they live have to do with it.
I am starting from the simplest case: marriage as the government sanctions and records it. That choice is about what can be counted, not about which relationships matter. Polyamorous relationships are not tracked here, and neither are domestic partnerships or other arrangements that fall outside a marriage license. Those would be valuable to add in future, as data allows.
With the marriage information in place for every county (how many people are married, how long current marriages have lasted, and how old people are when they first marry), I add other layers one at a time:

Economics: income, poverty, inequality, employment, and housing costs
Religion: the mix of religious traditions and the share of people with no affiliation
Political leanings: measured on more than one axis, described below
City size: from large metro areas to rural counties

The aim at this stage is descriptive: to see what correlations appear between marriage and each of these layers, before asking why.

title: Marriage, Religion, and Politics by County
section: Politics on more than one axis
text:
Politics on more than one axis
A single Democrat-versus-Republican number hides a lot. Two counties with the same vote share today can have arrived there from opposite directions, and a county where few people vote is not the same as one where everyone does. The pipeline therefore builds several separate measures from county presidential returns:








Dimension
Measure
What it captures




Partisanship
Democratic minus Republican share, 2020
The familiar left-right split


Realignment
Swing from 2012 to 2016, and from 2016 to 2024
Where a county came from, not just where it is


Participation
Turnout among voting-age citizens
Engagement versus withdrawal


Party attachment
Third-party share in 2016
Dissatisfaction with both major parties


Stability
Variation in lean across four elections
Settled versus volatile places



A principal components analysis then shows how many independent political dimensions the counties actually have.

title: Marriage, Religion, and Politics by County
text:
Method

PipelineReading the measuresTooling


The pipeline is a single R script that pulls every Census table in one pass, joins the election, religion, and rural-urban files by county code, and writes one row per county for Tableau.

Label check before any data is pulled. Each Census variable code is compared with the Census Bureau’s own label for it. A wrong code stops the run and prints the real table layout. An earlier draft of this project used misaligned marital-status codes that summed to 165% of the population; this check exists so that cannot happen silently again.
Marital status that adds up. The Census counts separated people inside “now married,” so the pipeline subtracts them before reporting the five categories. The run fails unless every county sums to 100%.
Connecticut. Recent Census files report Connecticut by planning region instead of county, which does not match the election or religion data. Connecticut is taken from the 2017–2021 estimates, the last with the historical counties.




Duration is a snapshot. It is the median length of marriages that are still intact, so counties with older residents score higher almost automatically. It is always read alongside median age and a separate divorce rate.
Small counties are noisy. Margins of error are carried through for the duration and age-at-marriage medians.
Places, not people. A link between a county’s religious makeup and its marriage patterns describes the county. It does not show that members of that tradition behave that way.



The pipeline was drafted with Claude and its Census codes are verified against Census labels at run time.

Conclusions

The divergence is universal. Every top-5 European league is more stratified in 2025 than in 1992.

Pre-Abramovich (1992-2003): The Fergie Monopoly
The early Premier League was dominated by a single manager. Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United won 8 of 11 titles, but the points required to win were not exceptionally high (average: ~83 pts). The league was competitive enough that Blackburn (1995) and Arsenal (1998, 2002, 2004) could break through.

The Oligarch Era (2003-2016): Money Changes Everything
Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea in 2003 marked a turning point. Then Manchester City’s 2008 takeover created a third “super-club.” Title-winning points climbed to an average of ~88 pts, while relegation survival drifted down to ~35 points.
The Leicester miracle (2015/16, 81 pts) was the exception that proved the rule.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
There is a principle, often attributed to the Haudenosaunee (the Iroquois Confederacy) and their Great Law of Peace, that the decisions we make today should take into account their effect on the seventh generation after us. For a long time I’ve mixed up its origins and credited it to the Menominee people of Wisconsin. I’ve since learned better, but the Menominee may be the most remarkable living example of the idea. They have harvested timber from their forest continuously since the 1850s, and today it holds more standing timber than when they began. They have taken from it for closing on two centuries. That extraction has been done with such wisdom and care that the forest after the forest has more not less.
I’ve usually understood the Seventh Generation principle as a limiting ethic of present decision and action. We should act responsibly today so the future can inherit something good. It’s a call to look ahead and to remember that our choices outlive us. All of that is true and worth remembering. Lately, though, I’ve started to notice another side of the idea, and it has interesting implications for social change.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
Turning the Timeline Around
Another way of reading the principle is that the change we are working for may not arrive for seven generations and the work that must be done between now and then.
Take an enormous goal such as ending world hunger. If I approach it expecting to see it solved in my lifetime, I’ll almost certainly end up either disillusioned or exhausted, and probably both. But if I accept that I’m one participant in a project that spans decades beyond my life, the work changes character. My job is no longer to solve the problem, to finish, to accomplish. My job is to continue faithfully, doing the steps I can do now and trusting that those who come after me will carry things further than I could.
That shift takes the impossible task of achievement off my shoulders and leaves me with the very possible task of contributing. There is an old saying, often identified as a Greek proverb, that a society grows great when people plant trees whose shade they will never sit in. I think the seventh generation view goes further. We aren’t only planting for others. We’re also tending saplings someone else planted, and passing along work whose beginning we never saw and whose end we never will.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
Change Without Heroes
What I find most important about this view is that it can be anti-hierarchical. A theory of change built on power usually needs a hero, a decisive moment, and a visible victory, all fitting neatly within one lifetime. That model puts a great deal of weight on the few people who hold power and very little on the many who do the ordinary work. I was often presented the story of Dr. King that way (and it still lurks around in my consciousness). Or consider the ways so many stories or movies are presented centering on an individual or small group. To tell a human sized story, that attention to the individual creates draw, empathy, attention. But does it distort our perspective around social change?
A communal, generational view of change needs none of that. It asks for slow, steady, patient work rather than brilliance. Change happens slowly with many hands, and because it’s built that way, I hope it tends to last. This view also pushes back on our habit of measuring a life by the results we can personally claim. Nobody in a seven-generation project gets to put “ended world hunger” on their résumé. And in truth, these sorts of projects towards justice are larger than seven generations, and knowing which generation to locate ourselves in takes wisdom.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
Patience Is Not Passivity
I want to name a tension here, because I feel it myself. Patience about the long arc of change has to sit beside urgency about the people suffering right now. A child who is hungry today can’t be fed by the year 2200. A generational perspective is never an excuse to postpone compassion. I’m still not sure how to emotionally reconcile these things. Instead, it is often a bouncing between the anger and sorrow of suffering mixed with the centering of self for endurance.

title: Planting for the Seventh Generation: On Patience and Social Change
text:
We Are Someone’s Seventh Generation
One last thought has stayed with me. If I’m working for the seventh generation after me, then somewhere back in time someone was working for me. My generation is the future that someone else hoped for and labored toward without ever seeing it. I think of the work of abolition, liberation, and justice that have happened in history. The expansion of voting to those without property, to nonwhite people, to women.
That doesn’t mean the world is finished or that their hopes have been fully realized. Clearly they haven’t. But it does mean we’re standing on someone’s faithfulness. That seems like reason enough to pick up the work, do our share, and pass it along in good condition, the way the Menominee have done with their forest for more than a century and a half.
